highlights:
# H200 GPU rental rates fell from around $7/hour to around $4/hour in three weeks. · 2026-06-04T00:00:00+00:00

H200 GPU rental rates fell from around $7/hour to around $4/hour in three weeks.

→ The reflex read is that AI demand is rolling over.
→ The structural read is something else.
→ Two explanations hold up. One does not.

What is real: the Blackwell generation (B200 and GB200) is ramping fast and displacing Hopper-class hardware. Hyperscalers and neoclouds are discounting older chips to keep utilisation up.

This is generational transition, not demand collapse.

What is also real: the physical buildout is lagging silicon.

Power, cooling, transformers, and data centre permits have not kept pace with the chip ramp. A meaningful amount of compute is sitting idle waiting for grid hookups, and that unused capacity is leaking into the spot market at a discount.
This is a bottleneck cycle, not a demand signal. Exactly the kind of dynamic the ΣDX Fund is built to track.

What is being misread:
→ A 35–40% move in a thin spot market over three weeks is not an index.
→ Enterprise contracts at major clouds remain locked at term rates.
→ You do not get a regime change from a short window of spot dislocation.

results.title: Analyze whether GPU/accelerator supply…
highlights:
Nvidia's H100/H200 supply has eased substantially by mid-2026, with prices dropping sharply and wider availability, while Blackwell (B200/B300/GB200) remains tighter with lead times stretching into mid-2026 in places. This reflects ramped production, shifts away from Hopper, and hyperscaler buildouts, though CoWoS advanced packaging and HBM memory supply chains continue to constrain the absolute latest silicon. [1] [2] [3]

- H100 cloud rental rates fell from peaks of ~$8/hour in early 2025 to $1.90–$3.50/hour (or lower in some cases) by early 2026, with further stabilization or declines reported later. [1] [2]
- H200 is now widely available; B200/Blackwell shows limited early availability with premiums and stretched lead times (e.g., into June/July 2026 for some deployments), though supply is increasing. [1] [3] [4]
- Nvidia has phased down Hopper production to prioritize Blackwell; on-demand capacity for various SKUs has been sold out in periods, with 1-year contract prices rising ~40% in some windows due to sustained demand. [3] [4]
- Packaging (CoWoS) and HBM remain chokepoints, but capacity expansions (e.g., TSMC ramps) are helping; 2025–2026 production estimates show millions of H100-equivalent chips annually from Nvidia alone. [5]

...

### Nvidia GPU Supply and Pricing Dynamics (Post-Dec 2025)

Nvidia has curtailed Hopper (H100/H200) production to prioritize Blackwell ramp-up, leaving net-new Hopper supply extremely limited. New cluster deployments remain booked through at least August 2026, with Blackwell lead times extending into June–July 2026. On-demand capacity is largely sold out, and one-year contract rental prices for H100 rose nearly 40% from October 2025 to March 2026 (e.g., from ~$1.70/hr to $2.35/hr in some indices). B200 availability is improving gradually via hyperscalers but remains tight overall. [1] [2]

Persistent upstream constraints include advanced packaging (CoWoS) and especially HBM memory. HBM3E prices rose ~20% for 2026 deliveries amid demand from Nvidia H200 and custom ASICs; AMD cited memory costs as a driver for planned ~10% GPU price increases in 2026. These factors have sustained or increased effective pricing pressure even as some older GPU spot rates showed volatility or modest declines in certain reports. [3]

- Implication for competitors/entrants: Hyperscalers and specialized clouds are prioritizing reserved or long-term capacity; spot or flexible access favors those with existing relationships or willingness to pay premiums. Alternatives (see below) are gaining traction precisely because Nvidia supply lags demand.

AI data centers in 2025 are dominated by three hyperscalers—AWS, Azure, and GCP—alongside specialized GPU cloud providers like CoreWeave and Crusoe. AWS leads with $100B+ investment and recent 44% H100 price cuts (~$7.57/hr per GPU). Azure offers the most diverse GPU selection with transparent pricing starting at $6.98/hr for H100. GCP provides highest GPU density (16 A100s per node) but at premium pricing (~$11/hr per H100). Specialized providers can be 40-60% cheaper for large-scale training workloads.

...

Amazon Web Services offers AI infrastructure through two primary GPU instance families. The P Family (including P5 and P6 instances) is optimized for intensive training and high-performance computing workloads, while the G Family (G4, G5, G6e) is tailored for graphics rendering, streaming, and inference tasks.

AWS provides multiple configurations for V100 GPUs, ranging from 1x to 8x GPU instances across various EC2 regions, with pricing starting from $3.06 per GPU or $24.48 for an 8xV100 instance. In June 2025, AWS announced a significant 44% price reduction on P5 instances powered by NVIDIA H100 GPUs across regions, bringing H100 rental costs to approximately $7.57/hour per GPU. For a p5.48xlarge instance with 8×H100 GPUs, the total cost is approximately $60.54/hour.

A key advantage of AWS is its Deep Learning AMIs (DLAMIs), which come preinstalled with GPU drivers including NVIDIA CUDA and cuDNN, popular deep learning frameworks like TensorFlow and PyTorch, and communication libraries such as NCCL. This pre-configured environment significantly reduces setup time for AI practitioners. AWS also offers substantial cost savings through spot instances, with potential discounts up to 90% compared to on-demand pricing, though with the caveat that instances can be reclaimed with short notice.

### Microsoft Azure GPU Cloud

Microsoft Azure has established itself as having the best selection of GPU instances among major public cloud providers. Azure provides GPU-accelerated virtual machines categorized under the N-series and NG-series, designed for diverse computing needs ranging from high-end AI model training and high-performance computing to virtual desktop infrastructure and cloud gaming.

Azure's H100 pricing varies by region, with the most competitive rates at $6.98 per GPU-hour for a single-H100 NC40 instance in East US, East US 2, and West US 2/3 regions as of October 2025. More expensive zones can exceed $9-$10 per GPU-hour. For A100 GPUs, Azure offers numerous configuration options ranging from $3.67 for a single GPU to $14.69 for 4xA100 instances. V100 instances range from $3.06 per hour to $12.24 for a 4xV100 configuration.

...

Google Cloud Platform offers six different GPU types that can be added to new or existing virtual machines, providing flexibility in configuration. GCP's A2 instances, powered by NVIDIA A100 GPUs, provide the highest GPU density among major cloud providers, with support for up to 16 GPUs per node. This high density is particularly valuable for large-scale distributed training workloads that benefit from low-latency GPU-to-GPU communication within a single node.

For H100 GPUs, Google Cloud's A3 instances (a3-highgpu-1g) are priced at approximately $11.06/hour per H100 GPU (1×H100 80GB in us-central1 on-demand), making them the most expensive among the three major cloud providers. However, GCP's pricing model for GPUs is more granular than AWS and Azure, allowing you to pay separately for the GPU and the underlying virtual machine, which can be advantageous for custom configurations.

...

## GPU Cloud Pricing Comparison

Understanding the pricing landscape for AI data center services is crucial for making informed infrastructure decisions. Pricing varies significantly based on GPU type, configuration, region, and commitment level.

H100 GPU Pricing (January 2026):

- AWS: ~$7.57/hour per H100 GPU (P5 instances, after 44% price reduction)
- Azure: $6.98-$10+/hour per H100 GPU (varies by region, lowest in East US)
- GCP: ~$11.06/hour per H100 GPU (A3 instances in us-central1)
- Specialized Providers: Typically 30-50% lower than hyperscalers

A100 GPU Pricing:

- AWS: Multiple V100 configurations from $3.06 to $24.48 for 8xV100
- Azure: $3.67 for single A100 to $14.69 for 4xA100 instances
- GCP: Component-based pricing, typically competitive with Azure

Cost Optimization Strategies: All three major cloud providers offer substantial discounts through spot/preemptible instance programs, with potential savings up to 90% compared to on-demand pricing. However, these instances can be reclaimed with short notice, making them suitable for fault-tolerant training jobs but not for production inference or time-sensitive workloads.

Reserved instances and committed use discounts provide 30-70% savings for predictable, sustained workloads with 1-3 year commitments. For organizations with consistent AI compute needs, these commitment-based pricing models can significantly reduce costs while ensuring capacity availability.

It's important to note that exact comparisons between AWS, GCP, and Azure GPU prices are challenging due to limited overlap in GPU instance offerings and regional availability. Pricing also varies based on instance size, CPU allocation, memory, and networking capabilities bundled with GPU resources.

Средняя стоимость месячной аренды GPU-инфраструктуры в России достигла 2,3 млн рублей, увеличившись за год на 64%. Рост цен обусловлен не только дефицитом мощностей, но и изменением характера задач: российский бизнес массово переводит системы искусственного интеллекта из стадии экспериментальных разработок в полноценный промышленный продакшен.

4 июня 2026 г. 1 056 прочт. 0

Объем рынка аренды выделенных GPU-серверов в 2026 году прогнозируется на уровне 17 млрд рублей с потенциалом двукратного роста. Аналитики MWS Cloud связывают подорожание услуг с увеличением стоимости оперативной памяти в 10 раз и скачком цен на продвинутое оборудование на 30–50%. При этом количество доступных серверов остается прежним, что создает дополнительное давление на стоимость аренды.
